guideSummary.surfnerd: 13th Street is a sand-bottom beach break at the foot of 13th Street in Seal Beach, right in the middle of Orange County. Most of the time it serves up fun, average peaks, but when a big winter swell lines up with good sand it can turn steeper and hollow. Plenty of better waves sit within a short drive, so this is more of a solid backup than a headline break.

guideSummary.surfnerd: 15th Street is a left-hand reef in Del Mar, a rare patch of rock ledge along a coastline made up of miles of beachbreak. It's the most popular and consistent break in town, with a fun, mellow character rather than anything heavy. The left peels along the edge of the reef and can line up for three or four turns, with an occasional shorter right off the peak.

It rarely serves up quality surf, and only a handful of days a year are genuinely worth it. A small crew of experts has cracked the equation, but this is no dependable go-to.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Anderson Street is a fickle Orange County beachbreak in Surfside that can turn on into high-quality, top-to-bottom A-frame wedges when everything lines up. It breaks over sand, and its quality leans heavily on swell refraction off the Huntington Harbor jetty. Constant sand migration and beach erosion keep the sandbars shifting, so peaks come and go, but the main break straight out front of the old water tower stays relatively dependable.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Anderson Street in Orange County is a fairly exposed sandbar break that has fairly consistent surf. Winter is the best time of year for surfing here. The best wind direction is from the northeast. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the optimum swell angle is from the southwest. Sometimes crowded. Watch out for - Pollution. Anderson Street

Swell wedges off the stone walls into hard-hitting A-frames that bowl through to the inside, and the wave can turn very hollow, powerful, and shallow. It faces south, so it sometimes holds a rideable wave when the rest of the coast has gone flat.

Out front you'll find a shallow beachbreak that runs fast and hollow, though it closes out more often than not. The real prize sits at the south end, where a rock outcropping sends off a hollow right on the right day.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Avila Beach is a mellow sandy beachbreak tucked into San Luis Obispo County on California's Central Coast. It's a quaint, out-of-the-way spot with two piers and rocks mixed into the sand, plus rocky Fossil Point down to the south. The surrounding hills are its best feature, keeping the water clean and glassy when nearby spots are blown out.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Cape Lookout sits behind the longest cape on the West Coast, and that headland shapes everything about the place. The water is about the cleanest and clearest in Oregon, and it stays a beautiful spot to visit whether or not it's breaking. It was once known for a quality righthand reef, locally called Boy Scout Camp, but geological upheaval wrecked that wave, and today the surf is mostly beachbreak with both lefts and rights.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Cape Lookout in Oregon_North is an exposed beach reef and point break that has reliable surf. Spring and Summer provide the best conditions. Ideal winds are from the east with some shelter here from north winds. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the ideal swell angle is from the west. Waves at the beach are both lefts and rights Surfable at all stages of the tide. It very rarely gets crowded here. Watch out for rips and rocks. Cape Lookout

guideSummary.surfnerd: Coos Bay-Bastendorff Beach is a user-friendly beachbreak and one of the central hubs of the Southern Oregon surf scene. Set along a coastline of rocky headlands and coves, this large, sandy cove is the first stop on the Cape Arago Highway, tucked between Yoakam Head and the south jetty at the entrance to Coos Bay. Yoakam Head shelters the beach from the regular south winds, and the peaks down toward the jetty are loosely divided into spots like South End, Gray Houses, Middles, and North End.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Bastendorff Beach in Oregon_South is an exposed beach break that has quite reliable surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat. The best wind direction is from the southeast. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the optimum swell angle is from the west. The beach break offers both left and right hand waves. Best around mid tide. It very rarely gets crowded here. Beware of rips, sharks and pollution. Bastendorff Beach

It rarely blows minds, but on a big, steep southerly hurricane swell it can flip into a genuine barrel fest.

It's a fun novelty wave and a welcome escape from the crowds at Uppers and Lowers, sitting in front of President Nixon's old estate.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Manchester State Beach/Alder Creek is a five-mile stretch of windswept, sharky beachbreak on a coast that faces northwest. That exposure means it takes the brunt of winter storm surf and just about every other swell through the year, which makes it a handy backup to check when Point Arena isn't breaking. It comes with a price, though: heavy rips, uneven bottom contours, littoral currents, undertows, and a nasty shorepound, so it's realistically a summer or tiny-swell spot rather than a year-round one.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Manchester Beach /Alder Creek in Mendocino County is a quite exposed beach break that only works when conditions are just right. Summer offers the best conditions for surfing. Offshore winds blow from the southeast. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the optimum swell angle is from the southwest. Waves at the beach are both lefts and rights. Best around high tide. Likely to be crowded if working. Beware of sharks, rips, rocks and locals. Manchester Beach

On 15ft-plus swells it arches into a near-perfect A-frame that's earned a reputation as the most rippable wave on the Big Wave World Tour. It gets towed more often than paddled, and the ride mixes beautiful carving walls and shoulders with short, high tube sections that have a habit of pinching.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Ventura Overhead is the standout at Emma Wood State Beach, where the coast bends between Ventura and the points and reefs beyond. It is a famous big-wave break that once served as training grounds for California's big-wave pioneers, and it still ranks as the area's premier big-wave spot. It only breaks a few times a year, but when it does it throws wedgy, open-face rights that funnel for hundreds of yards, along with steep, lined-up lefts that can barrel when there is enough west in the swell.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Winchester Bay/South Umpqua Jetty is a man-made righthander on the south side of the mighty Umpqua River entrance, where an Army Corps rock jetty reaches about 1000 yds (910m) into the Pacific. The jetty doubles as a wind block and lets sand pile up into bars, feeding a reliable, sometimes dredging right that peels away from the rocks in often classic form. It breaks over sand, and a rip usually runs along the jetty to give you an easy paddle back to the lineup.
